title: National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2018
short_title: National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would update and expand Australia's laws against espionage, foreign interference, and related crimes.
It would create new offences for covert foreign actions aimed at influencing Australian democracy, reform secrecy and sabotage laws, and add a trade secrets theft offence for economic espionage.

The bill would also amend the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act to allow interception powers for all new offences, and add an immunity provision for voluntary information given to the Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security.
changes: Creates new foreign interference offences targeting covert or deceptive actions by foreign actors.
Reforms Commonwealth secrecy offences to criminalise harmful leaks while protecting freedom of speech.
Introduces a new aggravated offence for providing false or misleading information during security clearance processes.
summary.affected: Australian law enforcement agencies, intelligence bodies, and people or entities involved in national security processes.

speeches.speaker: Malcolm Turnbull
speeches.brief: The speaker moved the second reading of the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and introduced the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Bill, which establishes registration obligations for persons or entities with arrangements or activities on behalf of foreign principals to provide transparency about foreign influence in Australia.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the two national security bills were initially flawed with overreach, threatening journalists, charities, academics, and civil liberties, but after extensive bipartisan committee work and 60 recommendations, the amendments now properly target foreign interference while safeguarding freedoms. The speaker also criticised the government's rushed process and lack of consultation, noting the bills were significantly improved through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

speeches.speaker: Anthony Byrne
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and related bill are necessary to protect Australia’s sovereignty and democratic institutions, asserting that the nation speaks with bipartisan unity against foreign threats. The speaker referenced Prime Minister John Curtin’s 1942 wartime address to emphasise Australia’s historical resolve, and noted that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (PJCIS) has included reviews and safeguards in the legislation.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Bill 2017, arguing their definitions of 'national security' and 'foreign influence' are too broad and could criminalise protest, whistleblowing, and reporting to international bodies. He also criticised the government's hypocrisy, noting that 12 MPs had been flown to China by Huawei while claiming to be concerned about foreign influence, and warned that Australia is becoming a "pre police state" with over 60 security reforms since 9/11.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 criminalises dissent, broadens national security definitions, and could jail protesters against projects like the Adani coalmine, while criticising the rushed passage of 50 pages of amendments without proper scrutiny.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: The speaker thanked parliamentary committees and presented government amendments to the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Bill 2017, arguing the reforms are the most significant counterintelligence changes since the 1970s and will introduce new offences for foreign interference, economic espionage, and strengthened espionage and secrecy laws.

speeches.speaker: Christian Porter
speeches.brief: A supplementary explanatory memorandum to the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 was presented, and government amendments (1) to (154) were moved.
